speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. MACALUSO    REFERENCE TO HEADLINE IN HAMILTON "SPECTATOR"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. It has to do with a newspaper report which appeared on page 1 of yesterday's Hamilton Spectator in which a story under the by-line of Mr. Tim Creery deals with a discussion between several Liberal M.P.'s and the hon. member for Labelle prior to his defection to the Conservative party.
I have no objection to the contents of this article, but the headline is misleading, unfair and damaging to the integrity of myself and the other hon. members mentioned in the story. The headline reads "Link City M.P. to Socred's 'Bribe' Claim". My question of personal privilege is based on two things, Mr. Speaker. First, any suggestions made by the hon. member for Labelle about a bribe were not directed to any of the M.P.'s involved in the discussions. Second, while Mr. Davey and all the hon. members concerned on this side have denied any suggestion of a bribe being offered, this matter has still to be looked into by a parliamentary committee. The headline, then, is wrong when it links my name or the names of any of the hon. members involved with alleged bribery.

maintopic: MR. LANGLOIS    PARTY DESIGNATION OF MEMBERS FOR LABELLE AND RIMOUSKI
MR. LANGLOIS    PARTY DESIGNATION OF MEMBERS FOR LABELLE AND RIMOUSKI
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker.
In Hansard of yesterday, April 29, 1964, the list of members of the house still showed the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard) and the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Ouellet) as being affiliated to the Social Credit party. I consider that to be an insult to the Social Credit party and a slight on all rightthinking members.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, that there be an immediate retractation and correction on the part of those responsible for such a disgrace, for we will no longer accept to be dishonoured by such ties.

maintopic: MR. LANGLOIS    PARTY DESIGNATION OF MEMBERS FOR LABELLE AND RIMOUSKI
speechtext: May I point out that I am informed a clerical error was inadvertently made, and that it will be corrected.

I wish to raise a question of privilege in connection with another matter which concerns a great many members of this house. I may say to Your Honour that this is the first opportunity I have had of raising this matter because I have just received a photostatic copy of the newspaper article in question.
This newspaper article appeared in the Toronto Telegram of April 20 and was written by one Lubor Zink, a member of the parliamentary press gallery. It concerned the appearance by myself on the C.B.C. television program "Viewpoint". I am not concerned with the observations of Mr. Zink concerning myself, no matter how unfounded and bizarre they may be, but I am concerned with one of the things said in the article, which is as follows:
I have nothing against the M.P.'s expressing their unavoidably partisan opinion over the public-owned C.B.C. and getting paid for it with taxpayers' money-
Mr. Speaker, I did not receive any fee for appearing on this program, nor have I ever received any fees from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is also my understanding that most other members of parliament do not accept fees for appearing on the C.B.C. I would draw Your Honour's attention that in view of the terms of the House of Commons Act this false allegation by Mr. Zink may well be defamatory, and I trust that either he or his newspaper, or both, will publish an appropriate apology and denial.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF GOVERNMENT ACTIVITIES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF GOVERNMENT ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house of certain decisions reached by the government concerning the organization of government activities relating to science and research.
Hon. members will recall that last December I asked Dr. C. J. Mackenzie to examine the activities of government relating to science and technology and report how, in his view, our efforts might be made more effective. On January 28 last Dr. Mackenzie submitted a report, a copy of which I now table in both French and English. I draw the attention of the house to the two principal recommendations put forward by Dr. Mackenzie in his progress report.
The first recommendation, which the government has now decided to adopt, is that a scientific secretariat be established to assemble and analyse information about the government's scientific programs and their interrelation with other scientific activities throughout Canada. This organization, which will be a small fact finding and analytical group serving in a staff capacity without executive authority, will, subject to approval of appropriate provisions in the next supplementary estimates, be established as part of the privy council office. It will, we believe, meet a long felt need in providing day to day support in the work of the privy council committee on scientific and industrial research.
Professor F. A. Forward, head of the department of metallurgy at the University of British Columbia, has agreed to serve as the first director of this scientific secretariat during its formative period. The establishment of the new office will take effect next July, and we count ourselves very fortunate in having secured the services of a man with the record, experience and ability of Dr. Forward. In creating this scientific secretariat, the government is also following substantially the course recommended by the Glassco commission.
The second recommendation contained in Dr. Mackenzie's report has to do with the proposal for a national committee on scientific policy, which again had been recommended by the Glassco commission. It will be noted from the report that Dr. Mackenzie in his report agreed in principle with this recommendation, but felt that before such an advisory committee could be brought into being we should re-examine the role of the national research council and define more clearly, in consultation with the national research council, what relationship should exist between it and the proposed new committee.
IMr. Greene.]

The government agrees that before a new advisory committee can be established the questions raised by Dr. Mackenzie in his report must be settled. This matter will therefore be the subject of study by the government, and in particular by the privy council committee on scientific and industrial research during the coming months, and it will be one of the first tasks of the new scientific secretariat to assist the privy council committee in this study.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, following a question of privilege which I raised yesterday, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in the absence of the Prime Minister, stated that an answer would be given today in order to clear up the confused situation existing between Quebec and Ottawa in regard to the national pension plan. The whole population is apparently wondering if we are going to have a double pension plan in Quebec or if the plan will apply uniformly across Canada. Could the Prime Minister enlighten us on this matter today?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CANADA PLAN-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON UNIVERSAL APPLICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to clarify this point again for the hon. member. I have already made a statement in the house which I thought was a clarification. I have also received a request for information along the same lines from the hon. member for Three Rivers, who was asked the other day to put his request on the order paper.
In reply to these questions I would say that the proposal we are making is that there will be one pension plan which will be the same for all of Canada. This plan will be embodied in federal legislation. But any province that

so wishes can pass its own legislation making the federal plan also a provincial one, which in that case will be administered by the provincial government.
However, as far as the public are concerned it will be the same plan, requiring the same contributions and providing the same benefits, whether it is administered federally or provincially. This, Mr. Speaker, is understood in the agreement that has been reached and the arrangements that have been made between the government of Quebec and the government of Canada. This, Mr. Speaker, is the proposal. Whether it is implemented depends on the will of parliament and of provincial legislatures, but it is a proposal in which the government of Quebec has concurred, which other provincial governments have welcomed and which I hope will soon be implemented.

Mr. Speaker, may I answer a number of questions to which answers were promised earlier in the week. The first question was asked by the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg with respect to differences between statistics provided by the unemployment insurance commission and the dominion bureau of statistics.
The most recently available figures on unemployment insurance beneficiaries are for February of this year, when there was an estimated average of 503,000 persons drawing 

benefits during the month. For the week ending February 22, 1964, there were 467,000 estimated as unemployed by the labour force survey of the dominion bureau of statistics.
The difference of 36,000 in these figures, both of which are estimates, can in part be accounted for by the sampling variability of the labour force survey and the estimating procedures with respect to the number of beneficiaries. The difference can also be accounted for because a number of unemployment insurance beneficiaries are working part time and drawing partial benefits, and therefore will not be counted as unemployed by the dominion bureau of statistics in the monthly force survey.
In addition, one of the estimates is an average of the number of people drawing benefits during the whole month, while the d.b.s. estimate of unemployment is a count of the number of people employed during the third week in the month.

subtopic: SARNIA, ONT.  ESTABLISHMENT OF BLUE WATER BRIDGE AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on Bill No. S-4, respecting the international bridge spanning the St. Clair river between the village of Point Edward and the city of Port Huron, Michigan. This bridge is known as the Blue Water bridge. A number of members in the house have asked me whether this is a new bridge, and to clarify the matter I should like to describe the background of the Blue Water bridge.
The bridge was completed some time in 1937. At that time the Michigan state bridge commission was formed and agreements were prepared regarding Canadian maintenance of this bridge, tolls, etc. The approaches to this structure, I might say, are in the most advantageous and commercially developed area of the village of Point Edward, Ontario. In the original agreement the village of Point Edward was to receive $5,000 in lieu of taxes each year. The original agreement did not provide for any Canadians to be appointed to the bridge commission although it is an international bridge.
The agreement further stated that when the bonds and debts of the bridge were retired the tolls would be discontinued. This took place in 1961. The original agreement also stated that when the bonds and debts were retired the taxes to the village of Point Edward would cease.
The present quandary in connection with this matter results from an obvious disparity in the legislation concerning this bridge. As I have stated, on June 1, 1961 the corporate

obligations of the commission were already satisfied and the commission took the position that by operation of law the portion of the bridge situated within the province of Ontario reverted to the Dominion of Canada and that all liability of the Michigan state bridge commission for taxes levied by the village of Point Edward or for any payment provided for in lieu of taxes would cease. Of course, Mr. Speaker, no taxes or payments in lieu of taxes have been paid to the village of Point Edward since 1961. I would also point out that when the original payment of $5,000 was agreed on back in 1938, operating expenses for the village were much lower than at the present time, and simple arithmetic will show that this very low payment is much too small and should be adjusted.
This Bill S-4 should be passed with all possible haste for the reason that the maintenance of this bridge has suffered, as well as the village of Point Edward. I am very gratified to note that this new Bill S-4 provides for the new bridge authority to consist of four Canadians and four Americans.
It has come to my attention, Mr. Speaker, that there is no maintenance staff looking after the Canadian side of the Blue Water bridge. Therefore unless immediate steps are taken to correct this situation there will be no grass cut, no painting or maintenance of the bridge, refuse will not be collected and the beautiful entrance to Canada from the United States will certainly be a mess. The surrounding area of my riding, including Lambton-Kent, is also very conscious that something must be done to correct this situation. I am sure my friend the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon) will agree with me that the passage of Bill S-4 is long overdue, and I would ask the house to pass it with all possible haste.
Mr. Mac T. McCutcheon (Lambton-Kent),
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to compliment the hon. member for Lambton West on his clear and concise statement in support of this bill. It is not often that I find myself in practically complete agreement with the hon. member for Lambton West, and in view of this I am forced to conclude that his thinking is changing for the better. In support of what has already been said I should like to add one or two brief comments as background to the bill.
In about 1928 the St. Clair Transit Company was incorporated under special act of the government of Canada. It was authorized to build, finance, maintain, operate, and charge tolls in respect of the Canadian portion of this international bridge at Point Edward, Ontario. The statute further provided that

upon the retirement of all corporate obligations of the company or of any person to whom it might assign its rights, the operation of the bridge within Canada should be conveyed to the Dominion of Canada. The St. Clair Transit Company subsequently passed out of existence, but prior to this time it assigned all its authority to the bridge commission of the state of Michigan.
The Michigan state bridge commission constructed the bridge and has, since its opening to traffic during 1938, operated and maintained it in a most efficient manner. It was operated so efficiently, in fact, that the capital debt of the structure was fully paid off on June 1, 1961.
No problems arose until this capital debt was paid off. However, at that time, due to a provision in the United States federal law and the insistence of the United States bureau of public roads, grants in aid of a Michigan highway project would be withheld unless the state of Michigan lifted all toll charges in accordance with the terms of the grants made by the United States federal government to the Michigan state highway department to aid in the construction of the Michigan approach.
Since that time, or I should say since 1962, the bridge has operated toll free. As of now they have run out of money. Indeed, in order to provide for the continued operation of the bridge until the government of Canada could act, the province of Ontario has voluntarily assumed responsibility for winter maintenance, snow removal, sanding and the electricity necessary for the lighting of the bridge. The government of Canada has kept up the customs and immigration buildings. Recently, in fact within the last few days, all the maintenance and supervisory staff have been laid off as a result of a lack of funds.
As the hon. member for Lambton West has pointed out, there are many other important aspects of this matter. For example, he mentioned the taxes due the municipality of Point Edward. However, the maintenance and upkeep of the bridge is very important. Here we have a great structure joining two great nations. Are we going to allow it to fall into disrepair because the federal government has not got around to setting up the authority with power to operate this essential public structure?
As a matter of interest, Mr. Speaker, may I say that during the period April 1963 to April 1964, traffic crossing this bridge was as follows: United States passenger cars in, 568,128; United States trucks in, 50,324; Canadian autos in, 519,400; Canadian trucks in, 14,707; total passengers in all vehicles, 3,959,179.

It is 1963-64. These figures could very well be doubled, because they refer only to vehicles entering Canada. One could assume that almost the same number of vehicles left the country. This, Mr. Speaker, more than justifies the vision of those who many years ago planned this great project. With all this traffic it is essential that the structure should be policed, that service vehicles should be available and that maintenance should be kept up.
The purpose, then, of the bill before us is to provide for the establishment of a commission that will be charged with responsibility for having those things done. I should like to point out further that this matter has received the closest scrutiny in the other place. May I appeal, therefore, for quick passage of this bill so the commission might be set up to operate this service in co-operation with its United States counterpart and to accept for Canada what, by law, belongs to Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Postmaster General) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to abolish the local delivery rates for first class mail and for all newspapers and periodicals other than those published more frequently than weekly: to establish a minimum rate of one half cent per copy to each separate address for all publications other than those to which local delivery rates apply or that have postage free privileges; to make the four cent a pound postage on specimen copies of publications subject to either the local delivery rate or the minimum rate, whichever is applicable, and to extend to certain cultural and technical publications the privileges now granted to newspapers and periodicals devoted to religion, the sciences or agriculture.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purposes of this resolution are threefold; first, to initiate legislation which if passed, and I hope it will be soon, will provide the Post Office Department with additional revenues by abolishing the local delivery rate, by establishing a minimum rate per piece, that is per copy piece, for other than daily, weekly or semiweekly newspapers, and by making the per pound postage rate on specimen copies subject only to the minimum rate or to the local delivery rate. The second purpose is to extend to certain cultural and technical publications relating to fisheries, forestry and other fields the privileges now enjoyed by other periodicals devoted to religion, the sciences and agriculture. The third purpose is to abolish the local delivery rates on newspapers and periodicals published less frequently than weekly.
The first of these three recommendations is in line with recommendations made by the royal commission on government organization, the Glassco commission. The commissioners made certain recommendations that revenues be brought into line with expenditures.
The second and third objectives are to implement in part the recommendations of the O'Leary commission with respect to these publications.
Traditionally the Post Office Department has endeavoured over the years to break even in its operations while at the same time

providing a satisfactory service at a reasonable cost to users of the mails. According to the accounting practices in use over the years, this goal would seem to have been achieved. If you look at the annual reports of the Post Office Department, even the one filed a few weeks ago, you will find that year after year there would appear to have been either a small surplus or a small deficit. In fact in the last 10 years you will find that five showed surpluses and five deficits.
Unfortunately the accounting system employed does not reflect the actual facts. A number of major services chargeable to postal operations are supplied by other departments. Chief among these is the cost of the accommodation provided by the Department of Public Works. In other words, the post office buildings and other so-called federal buildings that exist from one end of Canada to the other have been supplied free of charge, and even some of the services being used in these buildings are provided free of charge.
In addition, the superannuation account for postal employees has been a direct charge against the Department of Finance and not against the Post Office Department as such. This fact was brought out very clearly in the Glassco report. It is reliably estimated that after the inclusion of all interdepartmental credits and charges, including franking privileges and other things, the Post Office Department would have faced a net operating deficit in excess of approximately $37 million in the current fiscal year.
Steps have been taken by my predecessor and myself to adjust these charges where this could be done without legislation. However, the changes I have mentioned today, more particularly the one having to do with the abolition of the household or local delivery rate or, to put it colloquially, the abolition of the four cent rate, need the authority of parliament.
I should like to direct the attention of hon. members to the estimates for 1964-65 which were tabled by the Minister of Finance some weeks ago. I draw attention to page 351 where under the heading "Post Office" hon. members will see the following at the top of the page:
Approximate value of major services not included in these estimates.
Accommodation (provided by the Department of Public Works), $25,298,000.
The amount is slightly lower in 1964-65 than in the previous fiscal year.
Accounting and cheque issue services (comptroller of the treasury), $584,300.
Contributions to superannuation account (Department of Finance),	$8,510,500.
Employee surgical-medical insurance premiums (Department of Finance), $1,170,100.
Employee compensation payments (Department of Labour), $261,900.
Post Office Act
The next item is the carrying of franked mail. I am not referring to franked mail such as mail sent out by members of the House of Commons. I am referring to the mailing that is done by the Post Office Department itself which, if it did not have a franking privilege and was paying for the services it is getting, would involve an expenditure of another $1,008,000.
These amounts total $36,832,800. In addition to these amounts that are not included, and which have not been included in the estimates in the past, you will recall, Mr. Chairman, there were very substantial increases in wages and salaries to postal clerks, as part of the regular review, which increases were introduced in 1962 and made retroactive to a date in the previous year. They are carried into the estimates this year. They affect the estimates, but nevertheless when you are considering the position for the 12 months ending on March 31 they would distort the picture if they were not in the estimates.
When a deficit reaches the proportions it has in the case of the post office, a deficit that will be at least $37 million if we had not made any changes, it is a matter of grave and serious concern for all of us. If the post office is to operate within its revenues, as the royal commission suggested, we must not only continually examine our operating efficiency but we must continually study and up-date postal charges for the services being performed.
I believe there is general agreement that the postal service of Canada has established for itself and is maintaining a high reputation for efficiency in world postal service. This becomes more evident when one travels and has the opportunity to compare the postal services of other countries, even those of our neighbours to the south and those in western Europe.
A review of the Post Office Department services by the Glassco commission has produced a real tribute to the work of the department, as recorded at page 309 of volume III of the Glassco report:
"The Post Office Department has attained a commendable degree of efficiency."
Improvements are continuing in the postal services and it has been my privilege to visit post offices in large and small centres. My first visit was to the post office in Quebec city, which is one of the two most modem in Canada. Quebec and Halifax are regarded as the two most modern, although some equipment has recently been put in the Winnipeg post office, which is still more modern, and which is being used on an experimental basis. From Quebec I went to the air mail post

Post Office Act
office in the airport at Montreal, and I have visited post offices in London, Ontario, in parts of New Brunswick and British Columbia.
I think I am a reasonably informed person and I must confess I was very impressed with the job being done in these post offices by the men performing the duties of postal clerks, and delivering the mail. However, great improvements are still needed. Automation is being introduced in practically every modern postal system in the world, and we should introduce more of it in Canada, if we are to meet the demands of the modem day and age, and if we are to keep costs under a reasonable amount of control.
The one thing that struck me, even within ten days of the time I assumed office as Postmaster General, was that the rising costs of new equipment and the rising costs of wages have to be taken care of by an increase in revenues. There is a serious discrepancy in our rate structure. Even before the Glassco commission made its report, Mrs. Fairclough, when she was postmaster general initiated a study to see how the rate structures stood in relation to the services being performed. The report from this study was laid before my predecessor and, before he had time to deal with it, it reached my desk.
In the meantime, certain minor adjustments that could be made by the postmaster general were implemented by my immediate predecessor, and others more recently by myself. For instance, we have increased charges for registered mail, special delivery letters and money orders. They were increased on November 1 last year and will produce $1,875,000.
The postage rates on third class mail, c.o.d. charges, and the mailing of newspapers and magazines, which took effect on April 1, likewise will bring in a substantial amount, some $6,265,000. But even with these two increases we are still short very close to $30 million in what we need to bring revenues in line with expenditures.
The first amendment that is proposed deals with what is called the local delivery rate, and it is estimated it will bring in some $8| million per annum. I should point out that there are now two rates of postage on letters posted for delivery in Canada. When I say letters I mean first class letter mail, sealed letters as distinct from third class mail. There is a four cents rate for local delivery and a five cents rate for delivery anywhere else in Canada.
There was a great deal of merit in having these two rates when they were first introduced. The local delivery rate, as many of us will recall, was intended for letters that are posted and delivered in the same post

office. In other words, a letter was placed in the post box, picked out, and put in a private box in the same local post office. In fact the rate for this service was in force even before confederation. Today, with the extension of metropolitan areas, this same four cents rate will cover the delivery of a letter perhaps 25 miles away, a letter that has moved by automobile or by rail, and has perhaps gone through half a dozen different hands.
If I may make a personal reference here, my hon. friend the member for New Westminster wired me congratulations the day I took office as Postmaster General, and drew attention to the fact that from north or west Vancouver you could mail a letter to one side of a certain road in New Westminster for four cents, but if you mailed it to the other side of the road it cost five cents. This just did not make sense. It just does not make sense, that a letter which is put into the mail has to be sorted, put in a bag, transported, then re-sorted at the other end before delivery should pay only four cents. In addition, we have rural delivery services and letter carrier services, particularly in the metropolitan areas, where most of the four cent stamps are used, and these additional services increase costs greatly. It is interesting to note that those who are getting most advantage from this four cent rate are commercial firms. I think they account for the use of 55 per cent or 60 per cent of the four cent service. In the light of the deficit of $37 million, these firms are not paying their way; they are being subsidized by the taxpayers generally. When these facts, collected in part while the previous government was in office, were brought to my attention I had no hesitation in recommending that the local four cent delivery rate be abolished and that we have one first class delivery rate, a five cent rate. That is the first recommendation contained in this resolution.
A second one is the extension of a special rate to certain cultural publications and to fisheries and forestry publications. This involves an adjustment in the second class mail rates which combines benefits to the publishing industry with a fairer distribution of the postal charges. The first benefit is represented by the proposal to extend to the publications devoted to the fisheries, forestry, arts, literature, and so on, the special rate of lj cents per pound which is now granted to publications devoted to religion, the sciences, agriculture and to extend this special rate to small weekly, semi-monthly and monthly publications with circulations under 10,000. I do not think any member of this committee would argue that a magazine devoted to forestry or fisheries should not be treated in the

same way as a magazine devoted to the sciences or agriculture.
The O'Leary commission recommended free distribution privileges throughout Canada for the first 5,000 copies per issue of publications referred to as "non-profit cultural" and "little" magazines. I know that many members of this committee have gone into these recommendations in detail. I myself have made a study of them. You may recall that the report ties in this proposal with a test relating to advertising content. But how impracticable it would be if we were to make postal officials in all the different districts responsible for determining how much advertising material was contained in each of these publications. Determination of the profitability or otherwise of magazines is difficult enough even for chartered accountants, and I do not think an attempt should be made to pass that responsibility on to the Post Office Department. We have gone as far as we can in seeking to implement this recommendation of the O'Leary commission and we have done it in the way suggested in this resolution.
We also propose the repeal of the local second class postal rates. This proposal is also included in the resolution. The second benefit to the publishing industry is the repeal of the local second class mail rates for newspapers and perodicals published weekly or less frequently. The local second class rate is a piece rate. This does not apply to all the publications I have been referring to; but in some instances where charges are based on weight, we recover as little as one fortieth of a cent per piece. This is ridiculous today when so much of our work is taken up with the handling and distribution of mail. The largest part of the load carried by our postmen is made up frequently of mail for distribution of which the department receives from one fortieth of a cent up to half a cent. In other instances we were getting up to two cents. Now, by a recent change, we will be getting three cents. The charge today for such local deliveries is one cent for the first two ounces, one cent for the next two ounces and one cent for each succeeding four ounces or fraction thereof. These rates are imposed by weight-they are rates per pound-and as a result it is possible to deliver a Montreal newspaper in Winnipeg or Vancouver cheaper than one could deliver the same newspaper in Toronto. There is no sense in it. There should be a minimum rate applicable to each piece of mail rather than a poundage rate, and that is what is proposed in this measure.
The extension of this special low rate and the repeal of the local delivery rate will result in no great revenue to the post office. Actually it will mean a loss. We will lose about half a million dollars on this item, and
Post Office Act
recover some $450,000 from the introduction of a minimum rate per piece, so there is, in all, a loss of $50,000 or so to the post office. As it is, we are carrying this mail on a poundage basis, and until parliament gives us the right to make the change to which I have referred the anomalies that I have mentioned will continue. However, when the change is brought about it will have the effect of putting the operation as a whole upon a sounder basis. At the risk of repeating myself, I will point out that approximately 80 per cent of the costs incurred by the Post Office Department today are incurred in the handling of mail. The department has had to gear its operation to handle individual items as against bulk mail. We now wish to extend that minimum rate principle to certain kinds of second class mail.
I do not think there is much more I can say at this stage. I shall, of course, be glad to answer any questions which hon. members may raise.

At the outset, may I offer my congratulations to the Postmaster General on his new appointment. I hope he can avoid some of the pitfalls into which the former postmaster general fell, unless of course he has his eye on the vacant Senate seat in British Columbia. I may say we hope we may not lose the present Postmaster General because we feel he has the ability to do the work assigned to him if given the opportunity.
I should also like to pay tribute to the 50,000 persons who are responsible each day for seeing that the mail is delivered in good condition and on time. I believe the employees in this department of government are a dedicated group whose devotion to duty is the foundation of the Canadian postal service. It is a devotion of which Canadians can be justly proud. On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, no doubt there has also been a certain amount of frustration in the operations of the postal department for it has had two postmasters general within the past 12 months. The report of the postmaster general for the year ending March 31, 1963 was tabled on Friday, April 3, 1964. The Postmaster General has already made reference to this report. There was some discussion a number of days ago in the house concerning this report when I asked the Postmaster General a question and pointed out that the report contained a letter addressed to His Excellency Major General Georges P. Vanier, Governor General of Canada, signed by the present Postmaster General under date of September 1, 1963.

speechtext:
I appreciate that reply from the Postmaster General, Mr. Chairman, but would point out that there must have been considerable confusion within the department or these errors in the original report would not have occurred. I am also concerned about this, that while this report was ready last September 1, it was not tabled until April 3, 1964. Perhaps the Postmaster General can explain that at a later date. While I am dealing with this report, I wonder whether the Postmaster General will table the revised report-perhaps he has already done this-so that the sessional paper will be correct in its entirety.
The resolution before us deals with the elimination of the local delivery rate for first class mail and makes reference to certain other changes relative to mail other than first class. My understanding is that the only portion of this resolution to which parliament has to give approval is the increase of the local delivery rate on first class mail from four cents to five cents. I think the Postmaster General pointed out that this rate has been in effect since confederation; that is, the rate for local delivery mail has been less than the rate for mail outside local delivery since confederation. To me it would seem that the local delivery mail rate should still have a preference over the rate for mail delivered outside the local area.
In his presentation the minister mentioned the fact that in the city of Toronto this mail may have to go through a number of hands before delivery in that area, but I still fail to see why it would cost any more in the Toronto area. I think it would cost less to deliver in the local area than some piece of mail delivered from Toronto to his own city of Vancouver. I understand, also, that the other increases mentioned in the resolution went into effect or could have been imposed as of April 1 without the consent of parliament. If this is correct, one wonders why all these other changes were included in the resolution.
The last increase in local first class mail rates occurred in 1954 when the Liberal government of that day, after removing the excise tax on cheques previous to the 1953 election, imposed a one cent increase to offset the loss from the revenue on the tax on cheques. Prior to that increase the first class letter rate
for local delivery was three cents, and at that time it was increased to four cents. The previous four cents rate for mail delivered outside the local post office was increased to five cents. The previous increase was, I believe, back in 1942, so it appears that every ten years or more the Post Office Department finds it necessary to increase the rate on first class mail. The 1954 resolution was very clear and concise. It read as follows:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to increase the rates of postage on letters posted in Canada from the 1st day of April, 1954.
Then it goes on to say:
(a) on each letter for delivery within the postal area in which it is posted, from three cents to four cents for the first ounce or fraction of an ounce, and from one cent to two cents for each additional ounce or fraction of an ounce-
Part (b) of the resolution dealt with the increase from four cents to five cents. The resolution we are asked to approve today is, to my mind, a jumbled-up affair. The first three lines of this resolution read as follows:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to abolish the local delivery rates for first class mail and for all newspapers and periodicals other than those published more frequently than weekly-
I suggest, therefore, that if we accept this resolution in its present form it means that first class rates for local mail are completely abolished and there can be no more first class local mail delivery. I would hope, therefore, that the Postmaster General will give serious consideration to withdrawing this resolution and introducing a new resolution in a more concise form, similar to the one introduced in 1954 when first class mail rates were increased.
I believe the figures the Postmaster General was using in his remarks today were those for the year 1963; that is to say, the fiscal year ending March 31, 1964. Of course, he is the only one who has access to those figures. The figures I will be using are taken from the 1963 report of the Postmaster General. This report shows a surplus of some $3J million. We must consider that this surplus was obtained under the very capable leadership of the former postmaster general, Hon. Ellen Fairclough.
One also wonders why local mail was selected as the target on which to raise revenue for the postal department. Whom will this increase affect? First of all, it will increase to some extent the cost of living, for it is the small businessman and individual who will suffer the most under the increase. Local businessmen make great use of first class local delivery mail for mailing information to their customers, monthly bills, and so on. Again, Mr. Chairman, I wonder why

local delivery mail was selected as the target to be increased, because the Postmaster General's report shows a general increase in first class mail in the years 1961-62 and 1962-63. The increase for the 1962-63 fiscal year was $115,899.87, while fourth class mail for the same year showed a decrease in revenue of $40,900.45. There is an item showing loss from theft and fire amounting to $38,646. We hope the Postmaster General will be able to tell us, before this resolution is passed, what is the loss by theft up to the present time.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can answer that question very quickly. Our losses are limited to $100 per package, regardless of how much is involved.

I am very pleased that the Postmaster General has answered the question in that way, but we would also like information as to what has been the loss from thefts which have occurred within the last six weeks or so. In recent weeks questions have been asked of the Postmaster General regarding mail thefts occurring in the Montreal and Three Rivers areas, and the minister has been quite vague in his replies as to the amount of money stolen. I am wondering whether he is withholding this information. Is he afraid to divulge the actual amount involved, for by not doing so he raises the suspicion that the amounts are very large, possibly the largest of any mail robbery yet perpetrated in Canada. I have been waiting for a reply to a question asked on Friday, April 10. This question, as reported on page 2033 of Hansard, is as follows:
I wonder if the minister is able to give us any additional information regarding the unprecedented robberies from mail vans in the Montreal and Three Rivers areas. Can he assure the committee that mail clerks are now being given adequate protection, and are armoured express trucks now being used to carry large sums of money? If that is the case, is this being done only in Quebec or is the practice being followed in other parts of Canada as well?
The Postmaster General has made a reference to the increase being necessary in order to meet pay increases for postal employees. I do not think anybody would suggest that the employees should not have a generous increase, for many of these employees have been waiting a considerable length of time for this increase to come through; I for one believe that they are very deserving because of the nature of their work. However, the Post Office Department is not the only department of government which has had to face increases in salaries. I do not recall in any other instance that a department has been told it must produce sufficient revenue to pay for salary increases and changing working
Post Office Act
conditions. The Post Office Department is the only department producing revenue in this way, and apparently the public users of postal facilities are to be saddled with the increased costs.
The Postmaster General mentioned that the Department of Public Works supplies accommodation to post offices all across Canada. In many instances that is quite correct, but I am thinking of a revenue post office where the local postmaster is required to provide his own accommodation. The Department of Public Works supplies accommodation to most of the other government departments, and they are not expected to raise revenues within their departments to meet the cost of these accommodations.
Going back to the increase in mail, I am sure that many postmasters in their own post offices have been deluged with mail coming through which should now carry a three cent stamp. I am referring to unsealed letters containing printed matter. I know that the local postmaster in my area has been deluged with this type of mail. The senders of the mail are not quite familiar with the new regulations and are still sending this mail out addressed to the receiver under a 2 cent stamp. In the interests of efficiency and expediency in handling the mail the postmaster of the local post office attaches a card and expects the receiver of the mail to pay an additional 2 cents. When these increases come into effect I wonder if something could be arranged to provide more adequate information to the senders of this type of mail, so that they are informed of the proper postage. I know it becomes embarrassing to them as well as to their customers to whom the mail is sent.
I was pleased to hear the minister say that the rural weeklies are still going to receive certain facilities along the line of the postage rates they have enjoyed over a number of years. I feel that these rural weeklies are providing a service to the areas interested and should naturally be given some consideration in mailing rates.
There is one other matter before I take my seat, Mr. Chairman. I note that a new stamp issue carries a flag bearing three maple leaves on stems with a white background and a blue bar at each end. I hope the Postmaster General can inform us what this depicts. Does it represent a kite-flying activity on behalf of the Prime Minister for his design of a new flag for Canada? I will close my remarks at this point, Mr. Chairman, and I hope that some of these questions I have posed to the Postmaster General will be answered in the course of the debate.

Mr. Chairman, normally one might expect the minister to wait until comments have been made by other members, but in case other hon. members in the house might fall into error by statements made, in good faith, by the previous hon. member I think some of his statements should be corrected. Before making these corrections I should like to thank the hon. member most sincerely for his complimentary references to myself and, more particularly, for the well justified complimentary references to the nearly 50,000 employees of my department.
The hon. gentleman is in error when he says that the only part of this legislation which has tp be approved by parliament is the abolition of the local delivery rates. I can assure the hon. gentleman that if he reads sections 11 and 12 of the act he will see that every single item in this resolution needs the authority of parliament before it can be put into effect. The hon. member need only read section 11, which deals with mailing charges for newspapers and periodicals, to see most of these items. If he reads the resolution he will see the first part of it is confined to first class mail that is the abolition of the local delivery rate; but the second part deals with the establishment of a minimum rate of one half cent per copy to each separate address for all publications other than those to which local delivery rates apply, or which have postage-free privileges, and that necessitates a change in the act. The third part of the resolution concerns the 4 cent a pound rate on specimen copies of publications and is tied in with an existing section of the act, section 12.
The last part of the resolution, which deals with the minimum rate for cultural and technical publications, is again tied in with a specific subsection of the act, section 11(3). speechtext: It seems to me we are not going at this in the proper way. I feel we should give every opportunity for the making of opening statements on this resolution. Perhaps questions might be asked of the minister later on, and just now I should like to see the hon. member for Danforth.

In rising to comment on the resolution stage of this measure, I should like to join the previous speaker in extending
his department.
I recall that last year when the estimates of this department were before us, under his predecessor, I referred to working conditions and labour conditions under which the employees of this department operate.
I do not intend to review my position at that time on this resolution because I would be out of order if I did. I merely mention it because I wanted to indicate to the minister that since that time we have amassed considerable information relating to labour conditions and working conditions of employees of the postal department. When his estimates come before us, we will be looking to him for a fairly detailed statement of his intention, programs and policies to be inaugurated to alleviate the revolting working conditions within the post office itself. The minister has only been in office a short time, but I am sure he is cognizant of these conditions. We shall be looking to him, when his estimates come before us.
Dealing with the proposals before us now, Mr. Chairman, I may say that the members of my party will deal with various aspects of the resolution and I shall deal with only one portion which relates to the proposal to increase local rates by 25 per cent, that is from 4 cents to 5 cents.
I wanted to indicate to the minister that unless a great deal more information is available to convince us otherwise, we intend to oppose this as vigorously as possible during its passage through the house. The reason advanced for the increase is that it will increase revenues, for one thing. The minister has read to us a statement of some of the unseen expenses, buildings and other services made available to the post office, which indicate the cost, over and above the figure we have been given of $36 million. I presume the increase is intended, in some way, to meet this unseen deficit.
However, sir, the other reason advanced, as I understand it, is that it will help the minister in drawing the boundaries for local mail. His remedy is that instead of trying to draw boundaries he will make everybody pay 5 cents, and presumably that will be the simplest solution. I believe, Mr. Chairman, very few people will agree. The evidence that we are able to obtain indicates that first class mail already shows a profit. The figures made available to us, for example, for 1959 indicate that first class mail showed a profit of $35 million. It seems to

Post Office Act
me, Mr. Chairman, that if these figures are accurate, then first class mail today is not only showing a profit but is showing a sufficient profit to almost equal the unseen costs the minister outlined to the house.
This proposal is borne out in the Glassco commission report, the third edition, page 324, where it says:
The most significant facts emerging from the above table are that first class mail Is shown to yield a profit sufficient to carry all the other services and produce an approximate break-even.
If these facts are true it seems to me that in any attempt to deal with costs and deficits in the post office we should be leaving alone any classification of mail which is paying its own way and which in fact is already showing a substantial profit. It appears that the real deficit is when you get into the area of second class mail. Again the 1959 figures that are available to us indicate that this class of mail showed a loss of $26 million. Mr. Chairman, these are newspapers and periodicals that are well able to pay the freight and carry their own expenses. I really cannot understand why the users of first class mail should bear on their backs the burden of the unprofitability of second class mail.
From recent figures we understand that first class mail is carried at a profit of 1.8 cents a piece, second class transient mail shows a loss of 10 cents per piece and newspapers a loss of 4 cents per piece. What I would be interested in hearing is some explanation from the government for this subsidy to the newspaper industry. I really do not understand why this particular preference is given.
I recall that when this item was drawn to our attention by the Auditor General in the public accounts committee last year and we asked him why there was this subsidy of millions of dollars to newspapers and periodicals he smiled, and the only thing he could say was, "Well, this is the way it has always been done"; but no rational reason, no economic justification, could be given. Therefore as this legislation goes through the house we will be looking to the minister to convince us, if he can, that we should withdraw our opposition, because at the present moment it seems to me that if the people who use first class mail are paying a rate which shows a handsome profit they should not be further burdened by granting an even greater subsidy to newspapers and other publications.
Again referring to the Glassco commission, Mr. Chairman, they attempted to analyse this problem, and as found on page 326 they state the following with regard to this type of special treatment:

It dates from the early part of the last century when the general level of literacy improved to a point where mass media had an audience. In response to the public demand for current news, and because newspapers and magazines were the only means of reaching the public on a broad scale, governments adopted a policy of subsidizing the costs of distribution.
They go on to say:
Today, the situation is vastly different. Other media of mass communication have developed and the underwriting of publication costs by advertisers has substantially altered the economics of publishing. Publications have grown enormously in bulk in the past 100 years-the four page newspaper of the last century appears today with mammoth editions of over 100 pages-and the costs of the post office have necessarily increased very materially.
They go on to point out this interesting fact:
The advertiser, responsible for from 40 to 70 per cent of the content of many present day publications (90 per cent was noted in one case), has become a beneficiary of the government's policy of subsidizing distribution of second class mail.
They say they cannot go into the area of public policy in this regard but they do make this recommendation:
An annual grant be made by parliament in amount sufficient to cover the costs of the post office in handling second class mail, to the extent that such exceeds postal revenues arising from the rates set by parliament.
In short, they are urging us to withdraw this subsidy or in the alternative to bring it above board. They are saying that the government, rather than loading this cost on the backs of the first class mail users in order to justify this subsidization of the periodical and newspaper industry, should frankly admit it and put a specific amount in the estimates to cover it, rather than trying to hide it among the estimates of the department.
There is anoher aspect of this matter on which I should like the minister to comment. It arises from the avalanche of American mail coming into Canada for which our post office receives no compensation. The Postmaster General, in reply to a question asked by a member of our party, indicated that during 1961 and 1962 the deficit for handling second class mail from the United States addressed to people in Canada was $3,900,000. According to the royal commission on publications, Canada's loss on second class mail fiom the United States in 1960 was approximately $6 million on publications alone. How much it was for other printed matter was not stated.
It is estimated that in 1962 Canada imported printed matter to the value of $300 million, at least 85 per cent of which originated in the United States. To my knowledge there is no other comparison in the world for this relationship between two countries. We in Canada absorb 35 times more printed

imports per capita than does the United States. This has occasioned grave concern, for example, in the graphic arts industry. In one of their bulletins they point out the huge flow of printed imports year after year represented by incoming second and third class mail from the United States delivered without any remuneration by our Canadian post office. All postal revenue for this material goes to Washington because of the universal postal convention which compels us to carry United States mail without compensation. Since the flow from Canada to the United States is in no way comparable, our post office is saddled with a daily mounting debt in this regard.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that there is good cause for a re-examination of the relationship between Canada and the United States in this regard. I understand, for example, that the loss incurred by our post office on Time and Reader's Digest is $1,400,000 a year. To me it is incredible that we should be in the position of distributing these fantastically wealthy publications and carrying them in our mails at a loss. These are only a few of the points that I-

MAPS SHOWING ELECTORAL BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all maps, drawn up or deposited with the chief electoral officer or the representation commissioner, pertaining to the proposed redistribution of electoral boundaries in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I make it quite clear at the outset that the purpose of this motion is to procure all the information which, in my view, hon. members need in order to examine and intelligently discuss Bill C-72, which is already before the house. I wish to make it equally clear that in presenting the motion I do so without any desire whatever of casting doubt or criticism upon the work that is being performed in this regard by the representation commissioner who, I know, enjoys the full confidence of members on both sides of the house.
If these maps are being drawn up, they are being drawn up in accordance with a
Electoral Boundaries Maps statute passed by this parliament. The necessity for hon. members to have access to them is, first, to put an end to rumours that have circulated widely in the house and outside it with regard to what the maps really are, what they portend to be, and how the different electoral constituencies are being carved up.
It could be that some hon. members have seen the maps. I have nothing to say on that. Personally I can say I have not seen them, but among hon. members who have seen them there has been great discussion regarding the new boundaries. We must remember that if Bill C-72 becomes the law of the land it will be initiating something very new. It will not only be a redistribution but a real revision of every electoral district in Canada, carried out in a manner different from that used in the past, namely by the appointment of independent, provincial commissions.
The importance of having the maps is to be able to decide exactly whether or not the proposal contained in clause 13 of Bill C-72, which stipulates a tolerance of 20 per cent from the provincial average of population, is a reasonable proposition. How can that be done without having access to maps, whether they be definite or hypothetical, complete or fragmentary? At least they are maps which will give hon. members some indication how the constituencies will look if this 20 per cent tolerance is adopted.
Another reason for my insistence upon this motion is to put an end to the aura of speculation and rumour under which the proposed redistribution is couched. I understand that at the moment there are three sets of maps, each made up with a different tolerance or margin, upwards or downwards from the average. I am told one is set up with a proposed tolerance of 10 per cent, another with a tolerance of 20 per cent, and a third with a tolerance of 30 per cent or 33J per cent.

Thank you very much. I do indeed recognize the soundness of the ruling you have just made, and if I have referred to constituencies, to my own constituency in particular, it is in order to show why it is desirable that these maps should be before us. It was to show that if a certain tolerance is adopted, you have a constituency with a certain appearance; if another tolerance is adopted, the constituency has a different appearance. At a later date, the committee of the whole house will have to decide whether or not the tolerance of 20 per cent which was proposed is the best which could have been chosen, and it would be infinitely better I think if the committee in carrying out this task could have the maps before it. That is why I am quoting the example of the constituency of Pontiac-Temiscamingue where one set of maps would for instance, bring the town of Rouyn into the constituency and another set might bring in a large section of the constituency of Gatineau. I think that is pertinent information for the committee to have in its possession before reaching conclusions about certain aspects of this bill.
The purpose of this motion is to provide for members of this house the fullest possible information on a question which is of vital interest to them and to the country. I am asking for the production of this material so that hon. members, as legislators, may be sure that Bill No. C-72, to which I presume the house will give its attention again in due course, is a proper solution to the redistribution problem. That is the only reason. To summarize-I see I do not have many minutes left-let me say I think it will be useful

for the house to have these maps, first in order to put an end to a plethora of rumours and, second, so that members may have before them in diagramatic and vivid form material on the basis of which they can better decide whether or not clause 13, as drafted at present, is acceptable and fair to all concerned as the basis for redistribution and as a basis, also, for the work of the commissions which are to be appointed. When the maps are before the committee it can determine whether or not due regard is being given in the legislative proposal to the immense geographical and territorial differences which exist between some constituencies and others. If, with the maps before them, members of the committee can see that what is being proposed is absolutely unrealistic and incapable of being performed satisfactorily, they may then decide on some other course, some other tolerance, or some other way in which to act so as to give adequate representation to all sectors and to all people in Canada. If the maps reveal that because of very large territorial differences, because of physical obstacles, because of a large number of hamlets spread out over immense areas, hon. members who will be called upon to represent such constituencies would find themselves faced with a completely hopeless task, I say it will be the duty of the committee at that stage to decide on some other course in order to ensure to Canadians the best possible representation.

I had hoped that when we set our hands to this task and did it in the non-partisan spirit of taking this whole business out of politics and keeping it out of politics, we would go through with it and not start faltering half way. But I do say again that the publication of these maps will not end rumours. It will start more rumours and create more false impressions. The hon. gentleman said he wanted to get the facts before us. There are no facts at all in these maps, because they will bear no relationship, except purely accidentally, if they do at all, to what will eventually result from a proper redistribution if we pass the kind of legislation we are now debating in this house. All they could possibly do is make confusion worse confounded.
Therefore it seems to me that if we are sincere and honest in our desire to end gerrymandering for good and to take out of partisan politics the redistribution of the representation in this house, we will reject every kind of device which will make that more difficult. I feel sure that production of these maps would have that effect.

Mr. Speaker, I have stated on several occasions, both in the last session and in this one, that I think it is a high point in the history of the Canadian House of Commons that we have decided to take redistribution out of politics. I think the decision we took when we passed the bill in the last parliament appointing the representation commissioner was a tremendous step, and we can take pride in the fact that Bill No. C-72 which is now before the house was given second reading with unanimous support. It is because I am so proud of the decision that parliament has taken to put an end to redistribution by political committees on the basis of political considerations that I think we should go down the line with that decision, and on that basis I hope that the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau), after debate has continued a little while, will see fit to withdraw this motion.
It seems to me that to ask for these sketches-or transparencies, as I have heard them described-to be produced would not only add to the confusion in the way the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has indicated, but it would give the appearance of parliament wanting to keep its finger in the drawing of these maps. I listened to the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue making a very plausible case for our needing to see them so as to make up our minds whether or not we would support the legislation; but I would suggest that either we believe in the principle of independent redistribution or we do not believe in that principle. Either we believe in giving the matter to people outside parliament or we do not. Either we believe in the principle of certain tolerances and standing by them or we do not.
The hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue wants us to defer our decision on a matter of principle until we have seen what the results of applying that principle would be.

Someone says "right". I think that that is a mistake and is a retreating from the high point which we reached when we in this parliament, both with respect to the bill passed last session and on second reading of

Bill No. C-72 this session, decided to go for a non-partisan, non-political redistribution.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question. I wonder if the hon. member would tell us whether in his view the question of tolerance, whether it be 10 per cent, 20 per cent, 25 per cent, or whatever it may be, may be discussed without in any way affecting the principle on which this house has already agreed, namely that of independent redistribution? If the hon. member answers that question affirmatively, does he not think that certain documents and maps placed before the committee would be helpful in deciding whether one tolerance is right, or whether it should be some other tolerance?

I not only think the matter can be discussed without seeing the maps, but I think it can be discussed far better without seeing them. If we agree with the idea that we should approach representation by population, either we decide scientifically upon certain tolerances and stay with them or we admit that we do not believe in the idea and want to decide on a tolerance which will produce the kind of boundaries we want. That is what we have done in the committees which handled redistribution across the years of our history, and I think we should get away from that.
I should like to read two or three sentences dealing with this question of doing the job independently, which I think are classical statements and bear repetition. They are to be found at page 1651 of Hansard for April 18, 1950. My first quotation is as follows:
I say that the time has come to consider the adoption of a system of redistribution of constituencies every ten years as the population changes, not in accordance with political considerations or personal bias, but that scientific consideration should be given to redistribution on the basis of population by a commission composed of the chief electoral officer, the surveyor general and one judge or more. No political considerations would be involved in such a commission. I would place them in a position where they would consider the whole matter of redistribution without denying to parliament the final say in connection therewith.

My hon. friend says the Conservatives agree. Please note that the request made then was that this commission be put completely beyond political considerations. The suggestion was that the only place parliament should come in would be at the very end. To request that we now see these maps is, I submit, to suggest that we have some finger in the pie as far as the work of the representation commissioner is concerned, and that we are interfering in the job even before it gets started.
May I read one more sentence and then I suspect that hon. members will know whom
Electoral Boundaries Maps I am quoting. In the next paragraph the same speaker said:
I feel now, with redistribution at least two years removed, the time has come to look into the matter of establishing a commission which would be free from political considerations to determine this question, not with a view to the political outcome in the ensuing election but in order to assure that democratic procedure shall be maintained in our country.
I have taken those words from a speech made in the House of Commons on April 18, 1950, by the then member for Lake Centre, later prime minister and now the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). I ask hon. members to ponder those words, that clear clarion call for putting the drawing of the boundaries of the constituencies of members of the House of Commons beyond political considerations. Yet it is now suggested that even before we have passed this bill, while we are still considering it, we ask to see, and to have made public for all the country to see, the exercises which are being made before we finally decide whether we agree to the principle and before we finally decide on the tolerances.
I am opposed to this motion because I believe to vote for it would be to cast a vote inconsistent with the vote which this house has already cast on second reading of Bill No. C-72. I would also point out that this same bill contains a clause, clause 17, which provides for the commissions, once they have been appointed and have done their job, to hold public hearings and to make the maps public for everyone to see-citizens generally, members of parliament, whoever you will.
In this motion it is asked that we be given some special privilege ahead of time to see these maps. It is asked that something be done now, even before the commissions are appointed, and which the commissions are not supposed to do until they have surveyed the whole situation and done their work. I think we are not only confusing the public, but we are certainly putting the members of these commissions in a very difficult position if we are going to see these sketches, these exercises, ahead of time, because we will inevitably state opinions about them and confuse the whole situation.
I feel about this as I feel about every other aspect of this whole question of redistribution. I think that parliament has done itself proud in getting over nine decades of the worst kind of redistribution. I think that parliament has done itself proud in the unanimous decision which it has taken, a decision agreed to by all members of all parties, to go for redistribution by a completely independent body, and I hope we will go all the way through with this decision.

Electoral Boundaries Maps I am not going to get into another argument which has been raised in another connection; suffice it to say that as far this aspect is concerned let us be consistent and go all the way. Having decided that we are going to give the job to people whom we will not control or meddle with, or to people whose work we will not try to influence, let us stay with that decision all the way down.
This is a terribly important issue, basic to the whole constitutional set-up. I regret the matter is being delayed. This is 1964 and the last census was taken in 1961. It would be a tragedy, almost a treason to the constitution of Canada, if because of delays on this matter the next election had to be fought on the constituency boundaries which were drawn on the 1951 census. I am afraid that if these sketches are produced this would add to the delay. Hon. members would start complaining about what is going to happen to their constituencies-and that is an anomaly right there. The constituencies are not ours. We are concerned with the rights of the people of Canada. As I say, I think that anything that delays carrying out the requirement of the constitution of Canada for redistribution after every decennial census is treason to the constitution itself, and regardless of who is responsible for the delay, whether it is the opposition that is holding up the matter or whether it is the government that is not bringing forward the bill, I believe that we should get on with the job.
I deplore the delays and I deplore any move to retreat from the very highminded decision of principle that parliament has taken to put redistribution beyond partisan politics, beyond the kind of thing we have had for the last nine decades. Therefore I hope that when this debate is over the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) will be consistent with his vote on second reading of Bill C-72 and will ask that the motion be withdrawn.

Post Office Act POST OFFICE ACT

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Nicholson-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to abolish the local delivery rates for first class mail and for all newspapers and periodicals others than those published more frequently than weekly; to establish a minimum rate of one half cent per copy to each separate address for all publications other than those to which local delivery rates apply or that have postage-free privileges; to make the four cent a pound postage on specimen copies of publications subject to either the local delivery rate or the minimum rate, which ever is applicable and to extend to certain cultural and technical publications the privileges now granted to newspapers and periodicals devoted to religion, the sciences or agriculture.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at five o'clock I had been dealing with the submission made to us by the minister, in which he purported to justify the increase in the mail rates. I looked over his statements during the dinner hour and, comparing them with the information contained in the Glassco commission report, I find it very difficult to reconcile his statements with the information and recommendations given by the royal commission in question.
The minister's main contention is that the department needs more money and the best place to get it is from first class mail. He also made the submission that it was his intention to have each class of mail pay its own way; in effect, be self-sufficient. The minister then outlined some of the deficits that were not included in the estimates. Over the dinner hour I was reviewing the report of the Glassco royal commission as it relates to the post office, because it gives some interesting information concerning these two types of mail. On page 325 there is a table which summarizes the receipts and the disbursements of first class and second class mail. The first class mail shows a surplus of slightly over $35 million.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, interested as we might be in this, I think it would be helpful if the hon. member drew to the attention of the committee that those figures were for 1959.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS

Perhaps if the minister kept quiet and listened for a while, he would find out.

Post Office Act

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext: These were the most accurate figures at which the commission could arrive after undertaking a very careful method of analysis. If the minister would read it, he would see this is an attempt to be very very fair to his department. If he has other figures for later dates based upon the same statistical detail then let us have them in the house and we will be glad to examine them. I do not want him to impute motives to any member of the house.
