maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
To go on, Mr. Chairman, the figures in question show that first class mail had a surplus of slightly over $35 million, and second class mail showed a deficit of slightly over $23 million. The table on page 326 allocates between these two groups the unseen charges that the minister mentioned this afternoon, amounting to some $31 million. Even after these are allocated, still the first class mail shows a surplus of over $19 million and the deficit on second class mail climbs to $29 million. I really do not understand how the minister can tell us that what he is attempting to do in this legislation is anything other than force the people who use first class mail to dig deeper into their own pockets in order to subsidize second class mail. I would also like to know from the minister why he has ignored the recommendation of the Glassco commission in this regard, why he is throwing this recommendation out the window, because it says quite clearly;
-the imposition of an obligation to subsidize second class mail from its own pocket-
That is referring to subsidizing second class mail from first class mail:
-seems undesirable.
They make certain recommendations to the minister in this regard; that he should, rather than have this method of subsidization, be frank with the country and vote the mail subsidy in the estimates themselves. We will want some pretty cogent figures from the minister before we will be convinced that this is not the case. The commission came to the conclusion that the deficit in the Post Office Department roughly equated the deficit in second class mail, and I cannot for the life of me understand why we should be asked to pay subsidies to newspapers and periodicals and, more particularly, to the advertisers in those journals, because that in essence is what we are doing.
We have also asked the minister to outline to the committee what steps he intends to 
take, if any, to deal with the disparity between the large losses suffered on United States mail carried free in Canada and the extent to which this is offset by Canadian mail carried in the United States. I have outlined the tremendous disparity, and although this may not be easy, we feel that explorations along this line are more warranted than digging deeper into the pockets of those who use first class mail.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, we want to know what serious consideration the government is giving to the other recommendations of the Glassco commission in which are outlined very precise steps which it is felt will give a truer financial picture of the operations of the post office and will effect very far ranging economies. It is suggested, I know, by the commission that various government departments should be charged for the services they receive and should charge back for services rendered, rentals and matters of that kind. Until we have this information we do not have before us a correct financial picture of the post office and we simply cannot make an intelligent adjudication upon the proposals submitted by the minister.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext: We never have had.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext: As the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam says, we never have had this in the history of the post office. I would have thought that action along those lines would have been more becoming in the circumstances. I feel, in conclusion, on the basis of the evidence we have heard today, on the basis of the minister's statement, that no case at all has been made for increasing the rates on first class mail. It is clear, from all the evidence to which we have access, that it not only pays its own way but shows a very substantial profit. The real deficit at the moment occurs in the hand-out given by way of subsidization to second class mail, newspapers and periodicals; and until something is done in this connection we intend to oppose this move. We also want to hear about the United States agreement, and what the minister really intends to do in regard to the recommendations of the Glassco commission. Does he intend to honour them; does he intend to put them into effect, or does he intend to throw them out the window as so many other recommendations have been treated in the past? That is all we want to say at this stage, Mr. Chairman; but until we hear more we intend to oppose this move.

Mr. Chairman, as we are considering the resolution to amend the Post Office Act, I want to mention that our Canadian postal system is recognized as

one of the best and most efficient in the world, thanks of course to our postal employees who are qualified and to all this devoted staff looking after the delivery of mail throughout Canada and attending every day to the distribution of correspondence so that all Canadians may have the best possible service.
I take this opportunity to pay special tribute to one and all.
I see in this resolution that it is intended to abolish the local delivery rate, which would amount to a disguised tax increase.
Of course, I appreciate the requirements of the postal administration because, like all other fields, it is affected by the treacherous inflation resulting from a financial system which is basically wrong.
Fortunately, we have some hope for the future, because after counting all those who favour monetary reform, I arrive at almost 25 per cent of the members of this house.
It is obvious that the post office is not a profit organization; but I realize how difficult it is to get fair treatment in that service. I know that personally, because I was a postal employee after my studies and I know that, when I left the service, two men were hired to replace me.
I should like to mention the case of the Chicoutimi post office which, for more than three years and a half, has yearly receipts of over $240,000, which means that it qualifies as grade 12. Its turnover this year will probably amount to $300,000 and I think it would be normal to classify it the way it should be.
I avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate the minister who, I believe, is able to understand the problems that exist at the present time in his department, since his administrative genius is acknowledged, and I hope that these small details will be corrected in due time.
May I add that I am happy to hear that post offices will be built in my constituency, namely at Laterriere, St. Honore, St. Ignace and in a few other places. I hope that those projects will materialize as soon as possible.
In conclusion, I would like to point out to the Postmaster General the case of Port Alfred which I submitted to him recently. This town has been asking for home delivery for more than 15 years. I have set forth a fair solution which I think should win his approval.
That was all I had to say on this matter, Mr. Chairman, because I feel that we should take every means to enable the Canadian postal service to operate efficiently and give the best service possible.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, you are very kind. But I was just following in the footsteps of some of my fellow members whom you tolerated so patiently.
I am now coming back to the subject matter. I simply wanted to convey to the minister some ideas we wished to express, and blaze the trail for the future administration of the department, because, when a resolution with regard to the post office is presented to the house, we necessarily must deal to a certain extent with the postal service.
Before going straight to the core of the matter, I hope I may ask the minister a second question. Will he maintain the partisan custom in his department of consulting people entirely outside politics?
We have now received the departmental report, and I wanted to congratulate the minister tonight for issuing it. Yet, I somehow feel ill at ease commending him, more particularly when he says:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to abolish the local delivery rates for first class mail and for all newspapers and periodicals other than those published more frequently than weekly-
Mr. Chairman, I want to tell the house that the suggested amendment, and more particularly the last words I quoted, affect us, and especially our small local publications to a great extent.
To my mind, this motion is nothing but a new tax on local delivery in Canada. It is not just any tax, but a specific imposition on private business. This is another case of the small local business being the whipping boy for the large corporation. The small man will again pay for some nonsense or some extravagant expenses the minister or the post office officials will incur.
Mr. Chairman, it is rather strange that, as soon as a deficit is foreseen in some department, it is immediately compensated by a

Post Office Act
new tax. Not the slightest effort is made to scrutinize the budget to see whether something could be adjusted in the estimates. None at all. Instead of making an effort in that direction, as soon as a deficit is foreseen, the imposition of a tax is immediately suggested. Always the same scapegoat.
The small man is always the one who pays in the end. When I find that the annual report shows a surplus of $3,486,449.02, I wonder why a new increase in postal rates is being proposed, after a surplus has been made public. As a matter of fact, I think that this attitude is even less understandable than the tax itself.
I must point out to the house that such action is unfair, and that if this resolution is passed tonight, it will simply be discriminatory toward the first class mail, as well as toward all our local publications.
Once more, we forgot, maybe intentionally, the big newspapers, the foreign newspapers which flow into our country and for which Canadian people pay higher and higher taxes.
I am taking part in the debate this evening merely to mention that anomaly within our administration, and I suggest to the Postmaster General, instead of considering a new tax before going to bed tonight, to go over his budget and determine whether there is no extravagance in the salaries or if there are expenditures which could be eliminated in order to balance his department's budget because, in my opinion, it is the easiest budget to reduce. In fact, the Post Office Department is supposed to be administered, most logically without having the small taxpayer pay higher postal rates.
On the other hand, if the minister has a mania for taxation, let him tax the rich. In short, let him tax those who can pay. Let him tax the owners of newspapers with a large circulation or those who run American magazines. But he should leave alone-and surely once in ten years is not too much-the small local businessman, the small Canadian undertaking which can barely make ends meet in our towns but which is trying to do something for the province of Quebec.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are the few remarks I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister and I hope he will consider them seriously overnight.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I urge the minister to reconsider his policy concerning new issues so that a stamp may be issued to commemorate the centennial of the death of Sir Louis Hyppolite Lafontaine who was in a way a forerunner of confederation since, at one time, he presided over the destinies of the two Canadas with Robert Baldwin.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take this opportunity to make a few remarks about the resolution before us.
Like the hon. members who spoke before me, I would like first of all to congratulate the Postmaster General, because the administration of his department being undoubtedly a very important responsibility, to be entrusted with it by his leader, evidently bears testimony to the minister's administrative abilities.
I would also avail myself of the opportunity to express my appreciation and pay tribute to the numerous employees of the Post Office Department who discharge their duties and responsibilities with tact and efficiency.
I would have liked, Mr. Chairman, the present Postmaster General's predecessor to be in the house today, to hear his successor state that the deficit foreseen for the coming year will be around $37 million. As a matter of fact, last year, if we remember rightly, the former postmaster general who is sitting, today, in the other place, which is much more peaceful than ours, was blaming the deficit on the poor administration of the Conservatives who were facing him.
Well, we have at present a Liberal administration which foresees a deficit of about $37 million.
I would also like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that those who will provide the additional revenue that the Postmaster General is looking for will always be the taxpayers. It is said that last November increases yielded some $8 million and that it is not enough. During a period of one year, Mr. Chairman, 20220-177
Post Office Act
it is the second time that the Postmaster General comes forward to ask for additional revenue. Last November, there were quite large increases in some cases. For instance, registered letters rate varied from 35 to 60 cents; letters by postal delivery went up from 10 to 25 cents, that is an increase of over 15 cents; postal parcel rate went up from to 20 to 35 cents, while money orders went up from 20 to 25 cents. Since April 1, 1964, there was another substantial increase for what is called commercially c.o.d.'s. We must also recall, Mr. Chairman, that to send our wishes next December, we will have to pay 50 per cent more than last year.
Added to increases provided for now, it will be an amount of $37 million, according to the Postmaster General's figures, that the taxpayers will have to pay over what they used to.
May we point out that according to the minister himself, it is mostly commercial and industrial businesses which will have to carry the load of that new increase. It is hard to understand, Mr. Chairman, that in one office, the distribution of first class mail should be increased.
In view of all the boasting about their own talent as administrators we heard from those people now occupying the treasury benches, something on which they all agreed when they were in opposition, it would seem to me that the Postmaster General himself is also heading quite the wrong way in taking steps which will certainly result in an even higher cost of living.
I have no intention whatever, at this time, of indulging in a speech on this matter, but I cannot refrain from pointing out to the house that what the Postmaster General is now asking us to do will surely entail an increase in the cost of living.
I suggest that the Postmaster General should look for other means of getting the money he needs without adding to the burden of the taxpayer in general by an increase in postal rates as steep as the one he is contemplating, especially in view of the fact that it is the second one in less than a year.
Mr. Chairman, that is what I wanted to say. I am convinced that the businessmen and industrialists in my riding would not have been pleased had I let this increase in postal rates go through without telling the house that they oppose it.

Mr. Chairman, before this debate commenced I had hoped to receive a statement from the minister with regard to a question I asked him some time ago as

Post Office Act
a result of the increased cost of sending newspapers to husbands and sons serving overseas with Canadian forces. I am certain that the introduction of this measure by the Postmaster General is to increase the revenue of the Post Office Department, yet the total cost of this increase will be borne by Canadians and is a hardship upon the people of Canada.
With regard to these proposed increases in rates I should like to point out that the profits of the Canadian editions of Time and Reader's Digest for the year 1959 were revealed by the royal commission on publications to be $937,000 in the case of Time and $1,158,000 in the case of Reader's Digest. The unfair part of it is that the postal subsidy given to these papers, according to post office figures, show that there is a loss to the Post Office Department each year on account of handling the distribution of Time of about $600,000, and between $600,000 and $900,000 in the case of Reader's Digest, depending on the method of calculation. The inequity of this is that Reader's Digest, a United States publication, pays a rate of one and three quarter cents a pound. Star Weekly, a Canadian publication, pays three cents a pound compared with this one and three quarter cents for a United States publication. Our Canadian newspapers pay more than three cents a pound. I hope that during the course of this debate or when the Postmaster General answers questions he will give the committee an explanation of his reasons for this action.

Mr. Chairman, some of us had the pleasure of watching the Minister of of Justice last night on "The Nation's Business" when he was interviewed by or had a chat with the hon. member for Northumberland. He introduced an argument at that time which it seemed to me the Post Office Department and the Postmaster General might have considered before bringing this legislation in front of us.
The Minister of Justice painted the picture in these words: Yes, of course, the provinces are going to get, not 17 per cent but right up to 24 per cent under a certain formula, but we will not get less. It is going to be a bigger pot; there is going to be growth. We are not going to get less. He did not make any mention of the fact, which I suppose the Postmaster General will, that costs are going up, wages are going up, expenditures are going up. All we got from the Minister of Justice in connection with the new tax agreement was how wonderful it is. Everybody gets more and nobody gets less.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext: Pie in the sky.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY RATES ON PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
It was real pie in the sky. I should like to know why the Postmaster General did not give us some of this pie in the sky. The fact is he has given us a different kind of pie and it is quite an argument he has brought forward. If I may refer to a local setting, the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William are adjacent to each other and they were very proud last year, the chamber of commerce in particular and with some reason, that they had managed to get the local delivery rate between two cities. The post office authorities, the postmaster general at that time and everybody else were very pleased about it. Everybody was estimating how many thousands of dollars local businessmen were going to save because of this action. Everybody was saying: This is justice which should have been extended to us long ago because we were obviously paying too much for postage.
What comes along a few months later, with this magnificent, competent government that always does things so well? They have got the genius for administration, you know. Port Arthur and Fort William lose their little percentage of benefit, but it is all in the name of putting the books in better shape. The department is going to have things look better.
I received a letter a couple of years ago from the postmaster general at that time, William Hamilton, and I want to put it on the record because the minister has said nothing in his introductory statement to indicate that this situation does not exist. The situation that is portrayed by Mr. Hamilton is the real problem here. The minister will not come out and really say it is. Instead he is going to get money from first class mail that he should be getting from some other kind of mail. Mr. Hamilton's letter reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Fisher:
During the discussion of my estimates in the House of Commons you asked me for certain information breaking down, as between Canadian and United States publications and as between newspapers and other periodicals, some earlier information I had supplied covering revenues and costs in this field.
In this letter I will try to do so but I must immediately caution you against assuming any particular accuracy for these figures.
I take it he meant that he was giving accurate dollars and cents figures, and his point is that generally they are accurate but not in particular.
I should also point out that we have no breakdown whatsoever as between newspapers and periodicals such as magazines; for our purposes these are all second class mail and no analysis we have ever made has attempted to make a division between the two.
Regarding my caution on the accuracy of the figures, I think this is understandable. Millions of pieces of mail are handled every day and

any assessment of volume, class and so on can only be on a sampling basis. Furthermore, since the job is so big and tends to interrupt the normal flow of the mail we make our studies only at fairly lengthy intervals; the detailed cost ascertainment study, for example, is done only every three years.
Finally, the further one attempts to break down cost figures and obtain details, the more uncertain those details become. For example, I am inclined to think that our total allocation of costs as between various classes of mail and our over-all estimate of the volume in each class is reasonably accurate; when one begins to break down a particular class into further groups, it becomes less accurate for a number of reasons.
You will remember also the running battle which has existed in the United States for some time over the basic question of how costs should be allocated as between various categories of mail and this has applicability to our Canadian costing systems as well since costs accountants will always argue over the basis on which overhead has been applied to various categories and what are direct and what are indirect costs.
Within this framev/ork, you will remember that our cost ascertainment statements for the fiscal year 1958-59 show the following figures relative to second class mail:
Second Class Matter
Volume (originating)	531,148,888	pieces
Receipts	$ 6,189,125
Disbursements	27,879,068
Disbursements over receipts	$21,689,943
I gather that the figure for disbursements over receipts is now up to $26 million so far as these particular	categories are	concerned.
Based on surveys which were made in 1955 and 1956, we estimate that the Canada post office handles about 120 million pieces annually of publications mailed in the United States and having the postage paid there, and about 40 million United States publications which are mailed in Canada and have the postage thereon paid to the Canadian post office. Our estimate of the receipts from the latter is $900,000.
Our cost calculations have always been based on the principle that they disregard mail matter originating and paid outside Canada and subsequently handled by the Canadian post office for delivery in this country. This principle is based on the fact that most letters generate a reply and that therefore there will be an equal volume of this kind of mail into and out of the country. Thus, while it produces a lower figure for the actual volume handled than would be the case if mail originating outside Canada was also included in the volume figures, and therefore a higher cost per piece figure when the volume is divided into the total operating costs for a particular class of mail, there is an approximately equivalent benefit to the Canadian post office by the fact that about the same volume of mail is sent out of Canada and handled at no delivery cost to us by other countries.
These principles are universally accepted by postal organizations and are, indeed, the basis on which it has been possible to organize such a smooth flow of mails between most countries in the world without any one country demanding payment for the work it does for another country in so far as first class mail is concerned.
While we have applied the same principle to all the classes of mail, in the case of periodical publications it must certainly be admitted that a far greater flow comes to Canada from the United

It is somewhat like the sales tax on building materials. It is done by stages. First of all, an increase was imposed starting November 1, 1963: the point was to find $1,800,000 in round figures; then, an increase on certain postal matters starting April 1, 1964 which will yield for the department receipts amounting to some $6 million and, today, we are presented with the grand finale which looks rather like a cap. In quite a number of other countries the post office has been separated from government; it is no longer a department of government but is established as an independent agency of government. In that case departments of government, things like periodicals, and so on, have to make a profit on their own and have to make their regular contributions. Mr. Chairman, in attempting to put the question to members of this committee you phrased it as follows: "Shall the resolution carry?" I do not think it should carry now. I do not think it should ever carry because it is, as other hon. members have pointed out, merely an attempt to gouge one portion of the population of Canada in order to protect another portion. In keeping with the historical actions or attitude of the Liberal party whenever it has been the government of this country and has dealt with postal rates, that process of gouging and protecting has been in keeping with their tradition, namely the protection of their friends at the expense of the general population.
Earlier today, in an exchange between the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister, occasioned initially by an off-the-cuff comment by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, there was some reference to a summer recess. The Prime Minister intimated that if the business of the house was not conducted more expeditiously there might not be any summer recess. We realize that one party in this house, namely the largest one numerically which sits in opposition, has done its utmost to obstruct matters to the point of grinding parliament to a halt, without sort of being too open about it; but if the intimation of the Prime Minister is that we have to rush things through or there will not be any summer recess, then I think that at least the members in opposition-we know the government backbenchers, even though many are privately quite critical of the resolution before us, will not say anything openly or publicly because of the rule of rigidity which exists on that side-should be prepared if necessary to grind this parliament to a halt over this particular item now before us.
I say that, because it means precisely what I said earlier, that it is merely an attempt to gouge the average citizen, the fellows in the low income groups, the small businessman and the old age pensioner, who a little while ago got $10 a month increase but who now, if he lives in a large metropolitan area and wishes to write a letter to a friend of his on the other side of the city, has to pay an extra penny each time. It is a disgraceful situation. Maybe it is only a penny. Maybe the Postmaster General, paraphrasing the 
late C. D. Howe, instead of saying "What's a million?" says "What's a penny?" However, if one were to count up those pennies in the pockets of the old age pensioners, people on fixed incomes or on other types of pensions, he would find it totals many millions of dollars. This is all designed to protect the friends of the government opposite, who protect the government editorially in their various newspapers.
This is a disgraceful state of affairs. Those of us from British Columbia thought that our province had been sort of insulted when the Prime Minister shuffled his cabinet and demoted the present Postmaster General from his prominent position as minister of forestry. We in British Columbia thought that with his background and knowledge of forestry he would have been quite an asset to British Columbia in that position. We thought it was an insult when he was demoted, but perhaps we see the reason why now.
It may not be that members of the opposition are desirous of filibustering or obstructing or delaying this particular measure, and if that is not the general desire then there is not much point in attempting to do so. But from my own point of view in matters such as these, I think that every means possible within the rules of the house should be used to delay the passage of the resolution, to prevent the introduction of the bill and to attempt to defeat the bill. If in the process of delay, obstruction and objection to this very iniquitous resolution the government happens to collapse and we have an election on our hands then, whether or not the people of Canada generally are desirous of having an election, we should blessed well have one, because there is no better issue to go to the country on than an attempt by the government to gouge the little people of this country in order to protect millionaires and others in preferred positions.
I do not have much more to say, except to leave that thought with the committee. Once again I express my own regret and sorrow, and the sorrow and regret of the people at home that such a measure as this is before us at this time. If and when this measure is passed by the house I know there is going to be great wonderment why this phalanx of Liberal backbenchers, the nouveau Liberals with the new ideas, did not stand up and say anything about this matter in parliament. I am not going to mention the names of any individuals. This is certainly not in keeping with common practice or what is correct, but people generally will wonder why some of these people on the backbenches, including the Minister of Fisheries who has, I see, relegated himself to the backbench, did not get up and say something

about this measure. Is it because they are afraid? Is it because they do not mind whispering privately that they wish the government had not brought in this measure, but publicly they do not want to say anything? Where is this emergence of response between the grass and the brass?

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF WINTER WORKS PROGRAM
LABOUR CONDITIONS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF WINTER WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention the fact that a few weeks ago we suggested to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) that the winter works program should be prolonged in designated areas. The Minister of Labour did not say yes or no. He said he would take the matter into consideration. We do not often see a minister ready to take a matter into consideration and to study a suggestion made by a member of the opposition. For that reason I would like to congratulate the Minister of Labour because he agreed to study that suggestion we made, and he did so, but in the end we received the answer that there would be no continuation of the winter works after April 30.

Mr. Speaker, since the Minister of Labour has agreed to take the matter into consideration and to report to us, I would like to know what has taken place in his mind and in the minds of his officials between the minute he agreed to take our suggestion into consideration and the minute he answered no.
What were the arguments in favour of the extension of the winter works program in the month of May and what were the reasons against such an extension after April 30 in designated areas?
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I have come to the following conclusion. According to the estimates tabled recently, that would not have cost the government one cent more. Most designated areas have a


harsher winter than others. Applications for various winter works to keep the unemployed busy have been submitted by those areas in November, December, January and February. What is happening today, or rather what is going to happen tomorrow is that just because the work could not be completed in those designated areas on account of the severity of the climate, projects will come to a stop even though they have been approved by both the federal and provincial governments and the necessary funds have been allocated.
When one knows that in the ridings of Roberval, Lapointe, Villeneuve and others there are still today six, eight, 12 inches, even two feet of snow, that permission was asked to carry out various projects, for instance, in-stal sewage systems, dig trenches or pour cement for sidewalks, and that in some municipalities, such projects, even if they were approved-the hon. members for Timmins (Mr. Martin) and Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) tell me that the same conditions prevail in their ridings, as well as in a Liberal riding of the Gaspe peninsula-have to come to a stop, one wonders why. Those projects had been proposed by the federal and provincial governments; they had been approved, funds had been allocated, but they are stopped before completion because weather conditions make it impossible to keep them going.
However, those amounts were provided for in government expenditures.
And those designated areas get the same treatment as other regions, like southern Ontario, British Columbia, or southern Alberta, which are very much privileged because even in February, March or April, digging, street repairs and sidewalks projects can be carried out.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that there is discrimination against some regions in Canada, because the regions favoured by a better climate can take full advantage of that winter works legislation, while others less privileged in regard to the climate, can take advantage of it only to the extent of 40 to 50 per cent.
So, let the Minister of Labour try and give us an explanation on that score. I am sure that he could not do it because the climate is not the same all across Canada and all regions cannot be treated on an equal footing and be enabled to take full advantage of that federal legislation, because too many of those ridings are handicapped by the severity of the weather.
I am not suggesting that the Minister of Labour is responsible for the weather, but I do say that he should be clever enough to see to it that the act is amended so that it will take into consideration the various circumstances which may exist in different regions.

The Minister of Finance was the first one to recognize that the main problem in Canada was that of unemployment and that especially in certain regions, it was a regional problem of unemployment. Besides, did not the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) talk about various types of unemployment: regional, cyclical, structural, frictional and other unemployment. But it remains that unemployment is the most important problem, the first problem facing this country, and the Minister of Labour refuses to do his share by extending the winter works period in designated areas, where unemployment is most acute and where it would be most profitable.
There is still one more day, tomorrow. The Minister of Labour can still announce tonight that in designated areas the works already accepted and approved might be continued, but only the works approved in designated areas. By taking such action, he would prove his good faith and would show initiative at a time when this government lacks constructive ideas to fight unemployment.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF WINTER WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for Lapointe for his vigorous appeal for an extension in the municipal winter works program to cover the designated areas. I share with him an interest in this problem and in any proposal which may be used effectively to extend employment opportunities in these and in other areas of Canada.
However, one must not forget the original purpose of this program. As originally developed it was intended to provide additional jobs in the period of high seasonal unemployment in the winter months, when seasonal unemployment accounts for 25 per cent of the total number of unemployed. For the past several years the municipal program extended over a period of seven and a half months, and the practice in certain parts of the country has been to begin the work in the fall, reduce it in the winter months when unemployment was really high, and then take it up again in the milder spring months and complete the work. The effect of this was to destroy the purpose of the program which was, as I said, to create jobs in the period of peak unemployment.
This year we reduced the duration of the program from seven and a half months to six months and as a result we have created a much greater amount of employment over fewer months of the year. This has been the best year, ever. More jobs have been created in a shorter period of time and the province with the most definite improvement is the province from which the hon. member comes. So it has been a distinct success.

subtopic: REPORT TO UNITED NATIONS BY SECRETARY GENERAL

speechtext:
1.	UN peace keeping force in Cyprus, on the date of issuance of this report, will have been operational for about one month, that is to say, for one third of the time foreseen in the security council resin of Mar 4. This initial period has been devoted to the deployment of the force, to intensive efforts to prevent a recurrence of fighting and to contributing to the maintenance and restoration of law and order in accordance with the mandate given to the force by the security council. The commander of the force and his staff, during this period, have had the opportunity to become intimately acquainted with the nature and complexity of their tasks and the situation in Cyprus, and to establish contacts with all the parties concerned on the island. In this period, at least until last week end, there had been a relative improvement in the situation in Cyprus, in the sense that except for some sporadic fighting in the Kyrenia range area no-repeat "no"-major military clash has occured and situations which might lead to such major clashes were being contained. For such developments UN operation in Cyprus may claim no-repeat "no"-small credit. The outbreak on Apr 26 of serious fighting in the area of the Pentadaktylos range (Kyrenia mountains) is, of course, a setback.
2.	Ultimate responsibility for a return to normal conditions in Cyprus must, obviously, rest primarily with the authorities and people of Cyprus themselves, since normality can come about only as a result of a determination by the two communities, so many of whose members on both sides are now armed and active as a sort of loosely organized militia, to lay down their arms and seek to live again in peace. The relationship and the tension between the two main groups of the population continue to be a cause for gravest anxiety. Since UN force became operational in Cyprus, there have been a number of isolated incidents of shooting in which innocent civilians have been the victims, incidents which have been utterly senseless and are disturbing in their indication of an attitude of irresponsibility and callousness toward human life on the part of those doing the shooting. UNFICYP received reports of a large number of persons missing before UN operation began, and since
then further reports have been received that cases are still occurring of persons missing, whose whereabouts are unknown.
3.	UN cannot-repeat "not"-be indifferent to savage acts of this kind and I appeal in strongest terms to all concerned to take immediate steps to bring an end to them.
4.	UNFICYP, on its part, has the duty to take all possible steps available to it which might facilitate the resumption of normal life in Cyprus. It must seek always to prevent a recurrence of fighting, while also taking reasonable initiatives designed to lead to a return to conditions in Cyprus under which an ordinary man may move about freely and carry on with his day's work without fear or hindrance. Only slight progress has been made so far toward implementing this third aspect of UNFICYP's mandate. But much careful thought has been given to this aspect of the task and the conclusion has been reached that there are initiatives which can be taken by the operation holding out at least a hope for success, and that these must be undertaken without delay by means of intensive discussion and negotiation with the parties concerned. Toward this end, the mission in Cyprus needs urgently to be strengthened by the addition of a top level political officer, who, on behalf of SecGen, could conduct negotiations for the implementation of the program mentioned in para 10 below and outlined in annex I to this report. This need has been underscored by General Gyani, who for too long now has been carrying, with devotion and distinction, the dual load of commanding the force and conducting negotiations on a variety of essentially non-military matters. Nothing in this sphere, of course, has been done or will be done which would in any way impinge upon the efforts of the mediator to find solutions to the basic problems. I wish to reiterate my full confidence in both General Gyani and Ambassador Tuo-mioja as mediator. As commander of the force, General Gyani, with great ability and complete impartiality, has sought to make the force effective in the discharge of its mandates from the security council.
5.	General Gyani, in pursuance of my instructions and, indeed, in accordance with his own views, has consistently sought to achieve the desired and defined objectives of the force

in Cyprus by peaceful means, that is without resort to armed force, the arms of the force being carried only for clear purposes of self defence. Despite concerted effort by General Gyani and the force, and my own earlier appeals, fighting persists in Cyprus, with lives of Cypriots-Greek and Turk alike-being needlessly and pointlessly sacrificed. 1 wish here to emphasize my view that UN force was dispatched to Cyprus to try to save lives by preventing a recurrence of fighting. It would be incongruous, even a little insane, for that force to set about killing Cypriots, whether Greek or Turkish, to prevent them from killing each other. Yet, that is exactly the dilemma which is almost confronting General Gyani in Cyprus today.
6.	On the other hand, the force cannot- repeat "not"-stand idly by and see an undeclared war deliberately pursued, or see innocent civilians of all ages ruthlessly struck down by snipers' bullets. In view of the security council's objective of ending fighting, the action at St. Hilarion of the past few days is especially serious since it clearly was a planned and organized military effort.
7.	Both sides have given to General Gyani their versions of the present fighting situation and their reasons for it. Greek Cypriot authorities assert that the action was urgently necessary because armed Turkish Cypriots occupying positions in the hills of the sector were harassing Greek villages by firing against them, endangering lives of the inhabitants and preventing them from cultivating their fields and grazing their animals; because of the building by the Turkish Cypriots of an air strip at the bottom of the range, and the blocking by them of the Kyrenia road, the only access to Kyrenia. The Turkish Cypriots, on the other hand, justify their holding on to this area militarily because to the south of the range there are three main Turkish villages and in the north one, which, they assert, would be endangered and harassed if Greek Cypriots controlled the range.
8.	Moreover, General Gyani had no-repeat "no"-notice or knowledge of the action in advance, and therefore he could take no- repeat "no"-steps to prevent it. He immediately took up this question with the Cypriot authorities, pointing out the implications of a military action of this kind for the future status and effectiveness of UN force in Cyprus. Ever since the fighting began, General Gyani has been exerting every effort to stop the fighting and toward this end has been seeing top officials on both sides. On Apr 28, he received assurances of peaceful intent from both the president and vice president of Cyprus. The two statements in connection with these matters issued by General Gyani
in Nicosia on Apr 28 are appended as annex
II.	As of Apr 29, the fighting has stopped and quiet prevails. There was no-repeat "no"- interposition of UN force in this situation because the fighting broke out unexpectedly and an interposition under heavy fire would be neither feasible nor-repeat "nor"-helpful. The effort of the commander, therefore, has concentrated on bringing an end to the active fighting, which now seems to have been achieved.
9.	UN force, in view of its mandate to use its best efforts to prevent a recurrence of war, must do all that it possibly can to stop fighting. It has been seeking to do this by all means short of bullets, and it should be solidly backed in this endeavour by all members of UN. In this it has my fullest support. In this context, I also call attention to para 1 of the security council resin of Mar 4 (U/5575).
10.	The force was deployed in Cyprus because govt of Cyprus, the govts of Greece, Turkey and UK, and all of the members of the security council had reached the conclusion that there had been too much fighting, bloodshed and destruction in Cyprus and it should now come to an end. There was no- repeat "no"-assessment of blame for what had happened and none is made now. But there must be an end to fighting and it will surely become necessary to determine responsibility if it continues.
11.	It is the parties themselves who alone can remedy the critical situation of Cyprus. The authorities of the govt of Cyprus and the leaders of the Turkish community must, with a high sense of responsibility, act urgently to bring completely to an end the fighting in Cyprus, if that island country is to avoid utter disaster. This can mean only that high officials of the govt and the Turkish Cypriot leaders will voluntarily and immediately renounce recourse to force as the way to solution of the problems of Cyprus. That is the critical and decisive need at this juncture. Because it is so, I feel bound to appeal most strongly to President Makarios and Vice President Kuchuk to announce publicly, without delay, that, in accordance with the letter and spirit of the security council resin of Mar 4, and in view of the operational presence of UN force in Cyprus, there is no-repeat "no"-reason for further fighting in Cyprus and therefore they renounce it, calling upon their respective adherents throughout the island to heed their call. Then, UN force in Cyprus could begin to function effectively, for it could underwrite security for all, for both Turk and Greek Cypriot, and help to restore normal conditions of life for all Cypriots.

12.	The mere presence of UN peace keeping force in the island and its day to day efforts at the military level to prevent or stop armed clashes and to help in the maintenance of law and order are not-repeat "not"-alone enough to effect the kind of improvement in the over-all situation which can really bring about a basic relaxation of tension and a fundamental betterment of deplorable conditions of fear, insecurity and distress in which very many of the inhabitants of Cyprus now live. Such an improvement is also vital if the efforts of the mediator to promote a peaceful solution of the problem are to bear fruit. On the other hand, in the prevailing climate of mistrust and hostility, the communities concerned in the Cyprus problem are themselves often inhibited from taking the kinds of initiative which might lead to a substantial reduction of tension and conflict, and when proposals are put forth they are likely to be rejected-less on their merit than on the fact of their origin in one group or the other.
13.	Taking such factors as the above into account, and in particular having in mind the urgent necessity of making progress in order to avoid having the operation in Cyprus stand still and eventually bog down, I have formulated, with the assistance of the force commander based upon his experience of the past four weeks, a program of steps and objectives toward the implementation of which, I believe, UN peace keeping operation should now concentrate its efforts. This program, about which, as a matter of course, the several parties and govts concerned have been informed, will require the co-operation of all those involved as well as their good faith and their confidence in UN peace keeping operation, if it is to be effective in producing the improvements which all desire. I believe, however, that the security council resin demands no-repeat "no"-less than earnest co-operation from all concerned, in the interest of the people of Cyprus and of the maintenance of international peace and security. The program which I have in mind, and which is annexed hereto, is by no-repeat "no"-means exhaustive, but it can serve as a yardstick against which the govts and peoples concerned, and the members of the security council, may measure the progress that is being made towards the objectives outlined in the security council resin of Mar 4, and reaffirmed on Mar 13.
14.	In situations as complex as that now prevailing in Cyprus, the worst enemies are suspicion, fear and lack of confidence, breeding, as they so often do, hatred and violence. I believe that it may be useful, therefore, for SecGen of UN to make public at this particular time a program of reasonable objectives
which all parties should readily find it possible to support. I earnestly hope that on the basis of the practical goals set forth in this program, Cyprus, with the assistance of UNFICYP, may be able to move significantly toward peace and normality.

Objectives and interim aims of a comprehensive program of action for UNFICYP:
1.	The task of UN force, as given in the security council resin of Mar 4, is to use its best efforts toward the following objectives:
(A)	to prevent a recurrence of fighting; (B) to contribute to the maintenance and restoration of law and order; (C) to contribute to a return to normal conditions.
Efforts in any of these directions must, to have their maximum effect and durability, be made in a concerted manner, bearing in mind that (A) and (B) above are decisive steps leading to the over-all objective of the restoration of normal conditions in the daily life of the people.
2.	The following is a suggested list of some of the objectives that could be defined as part of the program of action designed to imple-hensive program of action for UNFICYP:
(A)	Achievement of freedom of movement on all roads in Cyprus, including the Kyrenia road.
(B)	Achievement of freedom of movement for all communities within the whole town of Nicosia and other cities under conditions of security.
(C)	Progressive evacuation and removal of all fortified positions held by Greek and Turkish Cypriots, with priority given to Nicosia.
(D)	Exam of the problem arising from the div that has taken place in the Cyprus police between the Turkish Cypriots and the Greek Cypriot members and the negotiation of necessary measures for their progressive reintegration.
(E)	The progressive disarming of all civilians other than the regular police gendarmerie and the Cyprus army by the Cypriot govt and the Turkish community. UNFICYP, if requested, would assist in facilitating and verifying the disarming and the storage of arms under conditions of security.
(F)	The control of extremists on both sides.
(G)	The formulation of appropriate general amnesty arrangements.
(H)	The arrangement of security measures and other necessary conditions to facilitate return to normal conditions and particularly of economic activity.
(I)	The facilitation of the return of Turkish Cypriot civil servants and govt officials to

their duties, including the public services, such as postal, telecommunications, etc.
(J)	The normal functioning of the judiciary.
The process of consultation and negotiation on these aims would continue side by side with the day to day efforts of the force to carry out its mandate.
3.	While efforts to make progress on the above points continue, certain interim aims should also be established and pressed in selected localities and on particular problems. The following are suggested:
(A)	The removal of emplacements, fortifications and trenches in selected areas of Nicosia with a view to repeating this measure subsequently in other areas.
(B)	A determined effort in selected areas of Nicosia to re-establish normality by returning to their homes, under UN security guarantee, refugees, as, for example, those from Hamed Mandres to Omorphita who would not-repeat "not"-carry arms, and attention to the development of a program for the rehabilitation of their dwellings.
(C)	A careful formulation of ways in which UNFICYP might be helpful in meeting the problem of the excesses by individual policemen in the course of searching and seizing civilians which at present causes much tension. Such a plan, which would largely depend on the use of UNFICYP police, would require a reliable system of reporting of abuses and a regular follow through by UNFICYP in every case, and would also require a high degree of liaison and confidence with all Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot members of the Cyprus police.
(D)	The institution of procedures for inquiry into every serious instance of shooting, especially when casualties occur, so that a full record of such incidents, the reasons and responsibilities for them, can be determined and maintained.
(E)	The elaboration of a plan for the reintegration, with UNFICYP assistance and guarantee, of the Turkish Cypriot policemen into the Cyprus police force, perhaps starting in one or two carefully selected Turkish Cypriot communities.
(F)	The use of UNFICYP good offices with both sides to improve the existing unacceptable living conditions through resuming essential public utilities and services and finally to ensure normal living conditions for the Turkish Cypriot community in tense areas, such as Ktima and Polis.
(G)	Initial efforts to facilitate the return of Turkish Cypriot officials and civil servants to their positions in govt service.
(H)	An appraisal of the possibility of establishing in certain areas Cypriot Greek-Turk-ish-UNFICYP joint patrols as a means of restoring confidence and promoting a return to normality.
(I)	Efforts, with UNFICYP if necessary providing security, to revive meetings of Greek and Turkish Cypriots, both official and non-official, and at all levels.

Statements issued on Apr 28, by Lt General PS Gyani, commander of UN force in Cyprus.
1.	Quote-The scale of and the manner in which the operations have been carried out by forces under the authority of the govt of Cyprus in the areas of Pentadaktylos range (Kyrenia mountains) on Apr 26 and 27, indicate that these operations had been preplanned. They were a complete surprise to UNFICYP as there had been no-repeat "no" -sudden developments in that area in the last three or four days, and more particularly because I had put forward proposals for a cease fire on the eastern side of the pass.
Quote-As such action can have serious implications regarding the obligations of the govt and the role of UNFICYP vis-a-vis the security council resin and the task given to UNFICYP, I discussed the matter with the president and have also sent a full report to SecGen. Unquote.
2.	Quote-His beatitude the president has told me that he wants a political solution to the problem of Cyprus under peaceful conditions and he wants peace and normality immediately in the country and that he is prepared to assist the UNFICYP in every way to achieve this aim.
Quote-Similarly his excellency the vice president has reassured me that peace and normal conditions to the maximum possible extent is his aim and he is convinced that peaceful conditions in Cyprus are essential to negotiate a political solution.
Quote-It is my firm belief now, that peaceful conditions can be restored and maintained in Cyprus and we in the UNFICYP will work relentlessly to bring about active measures to reduce tension and eliminate fear and assist in every way possible toward achieving quiet and peace in the island. I appeal to all the citizens to refrain from any action that would disturb the peace and to do everything possible to promote good will. Unquote. Text ends.
